data.title: Checkout latency is above SLO during traffic surge
data.customer_impact: Checkout completion rate is below the 99% service objective; customer-facing errors are active.
data.operator_note: First responder suspected payment-service, but this is unverified.
data.objective: Restore checkout success >=99%, p95 <=800ms, and critical services to healthy state.

plan.hypothesis: The checkout latency spike is caused by a transient overload or misconfiguration in the payment-service, leading to cascading delays in checkout-service, rather than a fault within checkout-service itself.

steps.objective: Verify payment-service health and metrics during the surge
steps.success_signal: Payment-service metrics show no errors and latency within acceptable bounds

steps.objective: Check inter-service call latency from checkout-service to payment-service
steps.success_signal: Call latency remains below 200ms and no timeouts

steps.objective: Inspect checkout-service logs for errors or timeouts when calling payment-service
steps.success_signal: No error logs; all calls succeed

steps.objective: Confirm that checkout-service is not the bottleneck by reviewing its own latency metrics
If payment-service is healthy, investigate upstream services (e.g., inventory, shipping) for latency spikes
If a downstream service is identified, apply a temporary rate limit or circuit breaker
steps.success_signal: Latency returns to acceptable levels and checkout success rate >=99%

plan.rationale_summary: The first responder suspected payment-service, and the checkout-service is downstream of payment-service. A surge in traffic can overwhelm payment-service, causing timeouts or increased latency that propagates to checkout-service. The evidence of customer-facing errors and low completion rate suggests a downstream failure. Investigating payment-service first will quickly isolate the root cause and avoid unnecessary changes to checkout-service.
